transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19 15:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Ethan Clark (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam Patel (BlueRidge - ML Eng), Aisha Gomez (BlueRidge - ML Platform Lead), Marcus Chen (BlueRidge - CTO)
---
00:00 Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick recap — we saw a spike in regressions after the int8 rollout on last Wednesday's batch, and some oddness with fp8 runs on longer prompts. goal today is to triage, agree next steps, and decide whether to rollback any config.
00:18 Liam: yep, thanks Ethan. we pushed the int8 profile to the staging cluster and some downstream tests started failing. it's around maybe 2.4% of requests but concentrated on a few prompt types.
00:27 Aisha: just to add, some of the failures are in the rerank flow where exact sequences matter. it's not catastrophic but it's breaking an internal acceptance gate.
00:35 Priya: ok helpful. when you say "prompt types" can you give examples, is it long-form doc synthesis or short completion?
00:41 Liam: mostly doc synthesis with bullet conversion, also some system prompts with long context — token lengths 1024 to 2048.
00:49 Priya: got it. we have two hypotheses: one is tokenization/permutation sensitivity after quantization; second is kv-cache warmup behavior causing subtle token differences on long context.
00:58 Marcus: are we sure it's quantization and not a pre/post-processing change? we didn't change the tokenizer on our side.
01:04 Ethan: good question. from our side config changed only in the model variant (int8 compilation flags) and minor scheduling at the runtime. Priya, do the profiling traces show ops that are at risk?
01:12 Priya: we saw a few operator fallbacks in the int8 path — a handful of matmul kernels fell back to slower reference code due to shape edge-cases. those fallbacks can alter numerical rounding and produce small diffs that cascade for some prompts.
01:25 Liam: that would explain why only certain prompts fail. are those shape edge-cases tied to sequence lengths?
01:31 Priya: often yes. for attention patterns where sequence length plus kv dims hit an alignment boundary, codegen chooses a different kernel. also fp8's dynamic scaling can introduce different zero-point handling.
01:40 Marcus: can we reproduce locally? our platform is similar but not identical; we can sync kernel flags.
01:46 Priya: yes we want a reproducible minimal failing case. ideally a 1-2 prompt repo with exact seed. Liam, can you share failing prompts and which model variant + token counts?
01:55 Liam: i'll dump 200 failing prompts to the sheet, include metadata: seed, model-revision, tokens, and expected vs actual.
02:02 Ethan: perfect. quick note — folks, some of the reports named Redwood "redwood-inference" as "redwood infer" in the logs — transcript might replace hyphens. ignore that.
02:09 Aisha: fair. so what are perf deltas? i.e., does int8 still give us the cost/latency wins we expected?
02:16 Priya: yes generally. across the baseline bucket int8 gives us ~2.2x token throughput improvement and ~40-55% cost reduction per token compared to fp16 on the same instance types. fp8 has similar or slightly better perf but is more sensitive to numerical drift.
02:30 Liam: but for the failing bucket we saw a 1.8x slowdown due to fallback kernels, so perf drops were localized.
02:36 Priya: exactly, fallback-induced regressions are the main culprit in perf/quality hotspots. also caching behavior — when kv-cache is cold we saw more differences, possibly from cache key rounding.
02:47 Marcus: do you have an immediate mitigation short of rolling back? can we pin to fp8 on those buckets or route problematic prompts to fp16?
02:55 Ethan: routing is doable — Redwood can route by policy (latency sensitivity, prompt bucket). we can set a temporary rule to use fp16 for the failing prompt bucket while int8 remains default. this avoids rollback and keeps cost wins for the rest.
03:09 Aisha: sounds good. is there any estimator to decide which prompts to route? we don't want to maintain long lists.
03:15 Priya: we recommend a small classifier or regex rules initially — e.g., if prompt length > 1500 and contains structured system tokens then mark for fp16. we'll provide heuristics.
03:25 Liam: ok heuristics would help. also curious on the eval side — were the regressions seen against our test set or new production traffic?
03:31 Ethan: both, but heavier in production. you had a smaller validation set that missed some edge cases.
03:37 Priya: actionably, we want: deterministic INT8 runs (no multi-threading, pinned rng) against an expanded eval set, plus trace-level operator logs for failing inputs.
03:48 Liam: we can do that. question: how long will deterministic runs take? we have a 1k prompt set — is that expensive?
03:54 Priya: with deterministic settings it's slower per token but still reasonable — expect ~3-4 hours for 1k long prompts on dedicated pool. we can preemptively bump capacity for the run.
04:03 Marcus: budget concern. can we get a time/cost estimate?
04:07 Ethan: i'll provide a quick sketch post-call. it's in next_steps.
04:11 Aisha: one more question on fp8 — are there known library mismatches (e.g. CUDA kernels, upstream fused ops) that cause bit-level differences?
04:18 Priya: yes there are a couple. sometimes fused attention implementations assume fp16/32 ranges and scaling heuristics in fp8 differ. when combined with quantized linear layers the dynamic range can clip differently, altering downstream logits.
04:30 Liam: that was my worry. are there guardrails we can put in the runtime to detect when dynamic range clipping happens?
04:35 Priya: we have a lightweight detector we can enable that logs per-batch scale factors; if the scale deviates outside thresholds we can mark the request for fp16 fallback automatically. we'll enable that for the debug run.
04:46 Ethan: ok, so to summarize tentative plan: 1) Redwood runs deterministic INT8 baseline and FP8 parity check; 2) Customer provides failing prompts and seeds; 3) Enable scale-factor detector and operator trace for failing runs; 4) If immediate business impact is high, route affected prompt bucket to fp16 until root cause fixed.
05:03 Marcus: sounds sane. rough timelines? we need the 200 prompts by Friday and the debug runs by next week.
05:10 Liam: i'll prioritize it. expect upload by Thu EOD.
05:14 Priya: we'll schedule the deterministic run Wed morning our time and share logs.
05:19 Ethan: i'll send the shared spreadsheet and the heuristics doc after this call.
05:23 Aisha: any blockers from security to enable debug traces? we have strict entitlements.
05:28 Marcus: yes, we can't open prod data broadly. we'll scope the debug runs to a redacted prompt set and we can allow token-level traces without PII.
05:36 Priya: understood. we'll work with your security team; we only need per-batch scale logs and operator ids, no raw user data.
05:42 Ethan: Qi — sorry, i meant priya — will also include a column mapping to your internal IDs to help triage.
05:48 Liam: quick aside — saw a note about caching/kv behaviour; is the kv cache shape consistent between int8 and fp8 variants?
05:55 Priya: in principle yes, but codegen differences can alter memory packing and alignment, which can cause different rounding in indexing. those are subtle but observed.
06:05 Marcus: ok. if we agree to the plan, what's the rollback plan? full rollback to fp16 or partial routing?
06:12 Ethan: full rollback is an option but disruptive. partial routing is lower friction — we set policy to route specific model-route(s) to fp16 or to a fp8-safe variant. we'll document the policy and help implement it.
06:22 Aisha: make sure the policy is auditable in the console so we can revert programmatically.
06:27 Ethan: yes, console audit logs and a rollout record will be created.
06:31 Liam: last technical question — do you have a quick way to compare logits deltas to find where divergence exceeds threshold?
06:38 Priya: we do. we'll compute per-token KL/divergence and flag sequences above threshold. that helps find exact step where drift begins.
06:45 Liam: nice. that will help narrow operator suspects.
06:48 Ethan: ok final notes: i'll send pricing and spreadsheet; Priya will run the deterministic baseline and enable detector; Liam will share failing prompts. we'll reconvene next Tue 15:00 PDT.
06:59 Marcus: thanks everyone.
07:02 Aisha: thanks.
07:05 (call ends)
